sentence: Amphotericin B characteristically produces renal tubular wasting of potassium and magnesium, and patients receiving the drug require aggressive electrolyte replacement throughout treatment. The tubular toxicity is a predictable accompaniment of the antifungal therapy rather than an idiosyncratic reaction, and it can be severe enough to limit the dose.

Voriconazole produces a distinctive constellation of adverse effects including reversible visual disturbance affecting colour perception and brightness, photosensitivity with squamous cell carcinoma risk after prolonged use, and periostitis with skeletal pain in long-term recipients, the last attributed to fluoride deposition. Hepatotoxicity is dose-dependent. Therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended given highly variable metabolism through CYP2C19, with poor metabolisers achieving substantially higher exposures and rapid metabolisers risking sub-therapeutic concentrations. The drug also produces neurotoxicity manifesting as encephalopathy, hallucinations, and rarely seizures at supratherapeutic concentrations.

Proton pump inhibitors used long term can produce hypomagnesaemia by impairing intestinal magnesium absorption, and the magnesium deficiency can in turn cause refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia, since magnesium is required for the handling of those electrolytes. The disturbance may present as tetany, arrhythmia, or seizures and resolves only when the drug is stopped.

Anti-IL-17 biologics such as secukinumab and ixekizumab predispose to mucocutaneous candidiasis through abrogation of the Th17 axis that normally controls fungal pathogens at epithelial surfaces. Exacerbation of inflammatory bowel disease has been observed and these agents are not recommended in patients with active Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis. Injection site reactions and upper respiratory infections are otherwise the most commonly reported adverse events.

Adenoviral-vector COVID-19 vaccines including ChAdOx1 and Ad26.COV2.S have been associated with a rare syndrome of thrombosis with thrombocytopenia, mediated by antibodies against platelet factor 4 with mechanism analogous to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Estimated incidence is on the order of one per hundred thousand exposures, with younger women at slightly elevated risk. Recognition relies on persistent headache, abdominal pain, or limb swelling beginning days to weeks after vaccination.

Gadolinium-based contrast agents used in magnetic resonance imaging were linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, a debilitating and sometimes fatal fibrosing disorder of skin and viscera, in patients with severe renal impairment exposed to less stable linear agents. Restriction of these agents and a shift to macrocyclic chelates have nearly eliminated new cases, illustrating how chemical stability of a metal chelate determines its toxicity profile.

Natalizumab, an alpha-4-integrin antagonist used in relapsing multiple sclerosis and Crohn disease, carries an established risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy caused by reactivation of latent JC virus. Risk stratification combines anti-JCV antibody serology, duration of therapy, and prior immunosuppressant exposure, with cumulative risk above two years of treatment in seropositive patients exceeding one per hundred in the highest-risk stratum.

Combination cough and cold preparations frequently contain an antihistamine, a decongestant, an analgesic, and a cough suppressant together, and their use exposes patients to the cumulative adverse effects of several drug classes at once, as well as to the risk of inadvertent therapeutic duplication when a separate single-ingredient product is also taken. Paediatric use of these combination products has been restricted because the risks outweigh the modest benefit.

subtopic: wound care and topical antiseptic toxicity
sentence: Topical antibiotics applied to chronic wounds promote the emergence of resistant organisms and can sensitise the patient, and their routine use on leg ulcers and pressure injuries is now discouraged. Bacitracin in particular, while perceived as benign, is a recognised cause of contact allergy and, rarely, of anaphylaxis when applied to extensively damaged skin.

Polypharmacy interactions, where the combinatorial complexity of five or more concurrent medications produces unintended consequences, are a recognised hazard particularly in the elderly. The cumulative anticholinergic burden of several medications each individually with modest activity can produce confusion, falls, urinary retention, and constipation that may be misattributed to the underlying disease rather than the regimen. Validated tools such as the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden Scale assist in quantifying this risk, and routine medication review with deprescribing when feasible is recommended in older patients.

Ergotamine and dihydroergotamine, older antimigraine agents, can cause ergotism, a syndrome of intense peripheral vasoconstriction producing limb ischaemia, and they are absolutely contraindicated with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, which can precipitate severe vasospasm. Chronic overuse produces a particularly intractable form of medication-overuse headache, and the drugs have largely been displaced by triptans.

Premedication with corticosteroids and antihistamines is used to reduce the risk of recurrent contrast hypersensitivity, but the strategy does not eliminate breakthrough reactions, and severe and fatal anaphylaxis has occurred despite an adequate premedication regimen. The protocol also requires several hours of corticosteroid pretreatment, which is impractical for emergency imaging, leaving a residual unmitigated risk in the acute setting.

Antiepileptic drugs can paradoxically worsen seizures, with certain agents aggravating particular seizure types, for example carbamazepine exacerbating absence and myoclonic seizures in some generalised epilepsy syndromes. Recognising that the anticonvulsant is the cause, rather than uncontrolled disease, is essential to avoid the harmful response of further dose escalation.

Vedolizumab, a gut-selective alpha-4-beta-7 integrin inhibitor used in inflammatory bowel disease, was developed with the expectation that gut selectivity would avoid the progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk associated with natalizumab. Several years of post-marketing experience have generally borne this out, with no clearly attributable cases identified. Upper respiratory infections, nasopharyngitis, and headache predominate among adverse events. Infusion reactions are uncommon. The slower onset of action relative to anti-TNF agents in moderate-to-severe colitis must be considered in induction strategies.

Serotonergic agents can produce myoclonus as a feature of serotonin toxicity, and the appearance of spontaneous and inducible muscle jerks in a patient taking serotonergic drugs is a recognised warning sign of an evolving serotonin syndrome. Myoclonus also features in lithium toxicity and in the encephalopathy associated with several other drugs.

Ketamine, an NMDA antagonist with anaesthetic, analgesic, and dissociative properties, produces emergence phenomena including vivid dreams, hallucinations, and dysphoria, particularly in adults. Concurrent benzodiazepine administration attenuates these reactions. Cardiovascular stimulation through sympathetic outflow makes ketamine useful in shock but problematic in patients with coronary disease. Chronic recreational use produces ulcerative cystitis with severe lower urinary tract symptoms, hepatobiliary disease, and cognitive impairment. The recent re-emergence of ketamine as an antidepressant has required navigating these long-term concerns alongside the apparent therapeutic value.

Oral bisphosphonates such as alendronate commonly cause oesophagitis and oesophageal ulceration, an effect that has shaped their administration instructions requiring the patient to remain upright and to take the tablet with water on an empty stomach. Beyond the upper gastrointestinal toxicity, prolonged use is associated with atypical subtrochanteric femoral fractures and, uncommonly, osteonecrosis of the jaw, the latter risk being far higher with the intravenous formulations used in oncology.

Proton pump inhibitor discontinuation can produce rebound acid hypersecretion, as the chronic suppression of acid drives a compensatory rise in gastrin and an expansion of the parietal cell mass. When the drug is stopped, the unopposed acid output can generate dyspeptic symptoms in patients who had no acid-related disease, paradoxically prompting them to restart the medication.

Pregnancy registries are an important pharmacovigilance tool for medications likely to be used in or inadvertently exposed during pregnancy. Antiepileptic, psychiatric, biologic, and several oncologic registries have generated substantive long-term safety data including for offspring neurodevelopment. The methodologic limitations include selection bias toward more closely followed patients, confounding by indication where the underlying disease itself may affect fetal outcome, and incomplete capture of early pregnancy loss that may be most informative about teratogenic risk.

subtopic: wound care and topical antiseptic toxicity
sentence: Topical lidocaine and other local anaesthetics applied to large areas of abraded or inflamed skin, as in extensive dermatologic procedures or burns, can be absorbed in quantities sufficient to produce systemic local anaesthetic toxicity, with central nervous system excitation followed by seizures and cardiovascular collapse. The intact skin barrier normally limits absorption, so the hazard rises sharply where that barrier is lost.

Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents including ranibizumab and aflibercept have revolutionised the management of neovascular age-related macular degeneration but carry procedure-related risks of endophthalmitis at approximately one in two thousand injections, retinal detachment, and traumatic cataract. Systemic absorption is small but measurable, and although the cardiovascular safety profile in elderly populations has been generally reassuring, a small signal for arterial thromboembolic events has been observed in meta-analyses pooling regulatory data.

Concentrated liquorice consumption inhibits the enzyme 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, allowing cortisol to act unopposed on renal mineralocorticoid receptors and producing a syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Severe cases have caused cardiac arrhythmia and rhabdomyolysis, and the effect is reversible only slowly after the offending product is withdrawn.

Chronic occupational exposure of operating theatre staff to trace concentrations of waste anaesthetic gases has been a longstanding concern, with older studies raising questions about reproductive outcomes, and it is the rationale for the scavenging systems that remove exhaled anaesthetic from the theatre environment. The hazard here falls on the providers rather than the patient.

Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost and bimatoprost are first-line in glaucoma but produce a characteristic constellation of ocular cosmetic effects, including progressive iris pigmentation that is irreversible, hypertrichosis and darkening of the eyelashes, periorbital fat atrophy producing a deep-set appearance, and conjunctival hyperaemia. The asymmetric effects when treatment is initiated in one eye are an aesthetic concern that should be disclosed prior to therapy. Cystoid macular oedema is an uncommon retinal complication.

Drug-induced liver injury is conventionally classified by its biochemical pattern into hepatocellular, cholestatic, and mixed types, defined by the relative elevation of aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase. The pattern carries prognostic and diagnostic weight, since a hepatocellular injury with jaundice predicts a higher mortality than a cholestatic one, an observation captured in the empirical rule known as Hy's law.

Codeine is a prodrug requiring CYP2D6 conversion to morphine for analgesic effect. Ultra-rapid metabolisers with duplicated CYP2D6 alleles may experience life-threatening respiratory depression at therapeutic doses, and several fatalities in nursing infants of ultra-rapid metaboliser mothers prompted regulatory restrictions. Poor metabolisers, conversely, derive inadequate analgesia. Tramadol shares the CYP2D6 dependence with the added concern of serotonergic activity that may precipitate serotonin syndrome and seizure risk independent of opioid effect.

Low-molecular-weight heparins are partly renally cleared, and their accumulation in patients with significant renal impairment produces an unpredictable increase in anticoagulant effect and bleeding risk. For this reason unfractionated heparin, which is not renally dependent for clearance, is sometimes preferred in severe renal impairment despite its less convenient monitoring requirements.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Dorsal root ganglion toxicity has emerged as a recurring finding in animal studies and some clinical programmes of systemically administered adeno-associated virus gene therapy, with sensory neuron degeneration that may be clinically silent or may produce sensory symptoms. The mechanism is incompletely understood and represents a class-level concern for high-dose vector administration.

Cenobamate, approved in two thousand twenty for focal seizures, has shown remarkable seizure-free rates in some refractory populations but carries a substantial risk profile including DRESS syndrome at standard titration rates, leading to a mandatory slow titration over twelve weeks. Somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue are dose-related. The agent shortens the QT interval and is contraindicated in familial short-QT syndrome. CYP enzyme interactions complicate concurrent use of oral contraceptives and other antiepileptics, requiring careful regimen review at initiation.

Intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guerin immunotherapy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer commonly produces cystitis, haematuria, and flu-like symptoms, but the live attenuated mycobacterial preparation can also cause disseminated BCG infection, a granulomatous sepsis that may involve the lungs, liver, and bone marrow. Traumatic catheterisation increasing systemic absorption is a recognised risk factor, and treatment of disseminated disease requires prolonged antituberculous therapy.

Paradoxical bronchospasm is an uncommon but dangerous reaction in which an inhaled bronchodilator or corticosteroid worsens rather than relieves airway obstruction, sometimes within minutes of administration. The reaction may reflect a response to propellant, excipients, or the cold aerosol itself, and patients who report worsening symptoms after their reliever inhaler require careful evaluation rather than escalating doses of the same agent.

Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, with target serum concentrations typically between 0.6 and 1.2 mmol/L. Levels above 1.5 mmol/L produce coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, and gastrointestinal upset, and frank toxicity above 2.0 mmol/L may progress to seizures and renal failure. Chronic therapy is associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and clinically significant hypothyroidism in roughly fifteen to twenty percent of patients, requiring regular monitoring of TSH and renal function.

Anticholinergic bladder agents reduce sweating as well as urinary frequency, and in hot environments or during exertion this impaired thermoregulation can contribute to heat intolerance and, in extreme cases, heatstroke, particularly in elderly patients also taking other anticholinergic medications. This cumulative anticholinergic load is an under-appreciated contributor to morbidity during heatwaves.

Exogenous glucocorticoid therapy, beyond its well-known metabolic effects, suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and the resulting secondary adrenal insufficiency can persist long after the drug is stopped. A patient with this iatrogenic insufficiency may appear well until an intercurrent stress reveals the inability to mount an adequate cortisol response, producing an adrenal crisis.

Topiramate produces a distinctive constellation of adverse effects beyond the typical anticonvulsant profile, including cognitive slowing, word-finding difficulty, paraesthesias attributable to carbonic anhydrase inhibition, weight loss, and nephrolithiasis through alkalinisation of urine and reduced citrate excretion. Acute angle-closure glaucoma may emerge within the first month of treatment and is a contraindication to further use. Metabolic acidosis is dose-related and clinically apparent in chronic use. Teratogenicity including oral clefts limits use in pregnancy and women of childbearing potential require effective contraception.

Failure to account for a patient's documented allergy during the perioperative period results in the administration of a contraindicated drug, and antibiotic prophylaxis given without checking the allergy record has caused anaphylaxis. The breakdown is one of information transfer rather than pharmacology, and it is addressed through preoperative checklists and verification steps.

Insulin therapy carries the dominant risk of hypoglycaemia, which is the principal limit on glycaemic control in type 1 diabetes and frequently in advanced type 2 disease. Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure or coma is more likely in patients with impaired awareness, in renal impairment, with concomitant beta-blockade masking adrenergic warning symptoms, and in older patients. Weight gain through anabolic effects, lipohypertrophy at injection sites, and rarely allergic reactions to insulin preparations complete the principal adverse effect profile.

Vasovagal reactions during or after contrast administration produce hypotension with bradycardia and must be distinguished from anaphylactoid reactions, which characteristically cause hypotension with tachycardia. The distinction is clinically critical because the treatments diverge sharply, vasovagal episodes responding to recumbency and atropine while anaphylaxis requires adrenaline, and misclassification can lead to dangerous mismanagement of an unstable patient.

Brimonidine, an alpha-2 agonist used in glaucoma, crosses the blood-brain barrier sufficiently to produce drowsiness, fatigue, and even apnoea in young children, and is contraindicated below the age of two. Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis develops in up to twenty percent of chronic users, often after months of uneventful treatment. Hypotension and bradycardia have been described particularly in older patients, mediated through central sympatholytic effects analogous to clonidine.

Strong adjuvants enhance not only the desired protective response but also the local inflammatory cascade, and excessively reactogenic formulations have failed in development because the injection-site reactions and systemic symptoms were judged unacceptable for routine use. The balance between immunogenicity and tolerability is a defining constraint on adjuvant design.

The handover of an anaesthetic case between clinicians is a recognised point of vulnerability for medication error, as information about drugs already given, infusions running, and doses due may be incompletely transferred. Structured handover protocols are designed to ensure that the receiving clinician has an accurate picture of the patient's pharmacologic state.

Several antibiotics require dose reduction in renal impairment not only to avoid systemic toxicity but specifically to prevent neurotoxicity. Beta-lactams, particularly cefepime and the carbapenems, can accumulate in renal failure and produce encephalopathy, myoclonus, and non-convulsive status epilepticus, a presentation easily mistaken for the sepsis or underlying illness being treated.

Prochlorperazine and promethazine, phenothiazine antiemetics, can produce acute dystonic reactions, particularly in younger patients, with oculogyric crisis and torticollis appearing dramatically within hours of a dose. Intravenous promethazine carries a specific hazard of severe tissue injury and gangrene if it extravasates or is inadvertently given intra-arterially, which has prompted warnings about its mode of administration.

Anticholinergic burden in older adults is the cumulative effect of many commonly prescribed medications, each with modest anticholinergic activity. Tricyclic antidepressants, oxybutynin and other urinary antimuscarinics, antihistamines, certain antipsychotics, and even some cardiac medications contribute. The cumulative burden produces dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion, and falls, with several validated scales attempting to quantify the risk. Deprescribing of unnecessary anticholinergic medications is a key element of geriatric pharmacotherapy review and may reverse cognitive impairment attributed previously to early dementia.

Statins are generally well tolerated, but a small minority of patients develop myalgia or, much more rarely, rhabdomyolysis with creatine kinase elevations greater than ten times the upper limit of normal. Risk factors include high-dose simvastatin, advanced age, hypothyroidism, and concurrent inhibitors of CYP3A4 such as macrolide antibiotics or certain calcium channel blockers. Statin-associated autoimmune myopathy is a rare but distinct entity that persists after drug cessation.

Errors of omission, such as the failure to administer venous thromboembolism prophylaxis or to give a scheduled antibiotic redose during a long operation, are less visible than errors of commission but contribute substantially to perioperative harm. The absent action produces no immediate event, so the consequence appears only later as a preventable complication.

Drugs can also produce iatrogenic hypoglycaemia, and beyond the obvious case of insulin and sulfonylurea overdose, agents such as quinine, certain fluoroquinolones, and pentamidine have provoked dangerous falls in blood glucose. The hypoglycaemia from long-acting sulfonylureas can be prolonged and recurrent, requiring extended monitoring and treatment well beyond the initial correction.

Triple therapy, the combination of an oral anticoagulant with dual antiplatelet therapy in patients who have both atrial fibrillation and a recent coronary stent, produces a particularly high bleeding risk, and contemporary practice has moved toward shortening or de-escalating this regimen to limit the haemorrhagic exposure while preserving thrombotic protection.

Dopaminergic therapy for Parkinson disease produces its own movement disorder in the form of levodopa-induced dyskinesias, choreiform and dystonic movements that emerge after years of treatment and that fluctuate with plasma drug concentration. Managing the patient between the immobility of the underlying disease and the dyskinesia of its treatment is a defining therapeutic challenge of advanced Parkinson disease.

Valproate exposure in utero produces a syndrome of fetal anticonvulsant exposure with characteristic craniofacial features, neural tube defects, cardiac malformations, and impaired neurodevelopmental outcome including reduced IQ measured in school-age children. The drug now carries a contraindication during pregnancy across most jurisdictions, although the management of women of childbearing potential with epilepsy who have failed alternative agents remains clinically difficult. Pregnancy prevention programmes attempt to reduce inadvertent exposure but cannot eliminate it without removing the drug entirely.

Emergence from sevoflurane anaesthesia, particularly in young children, is associated with a high incidence of agitated emergence delirium, a distressing and potentially injurious state. The propensity of this agent to provoke emergence delirium is one consideration weighed against its otherwise favourable properties for paediatric inhalational induction.

Antidepressant treatment carries a recognised, if uncommon, risk of paradoxically increasing suicidal ideation, particularly in adolescents and young adults during the early weeks of therapy, a finding that prompted a regulatory boxed warning. The phenomenon underlies the recommendation for close monitoring during the initiation of antidepressant treatment in younger patients.

Chloramphenicol may produce grey baby syndrome in neonates, a cardiovascular collapse with abdominal distension and ashen colour that reflects immature glucuronidation and inadequate clearance of the drug. This pharmacokinetic vulnerability of neonates is paradigmatic of the broader principle that paediatric dosing cannot be simply scaled by body weight from adult equivalents and that age-specific enzyme maturation must be considered. The drug is now rarely used in neonates and only at carefully selected dosing where serum concentration monitoring is available.

Cumulative cardiovascular polypharmacy in older adults often includes an antihypertensive regimen, statin, antiplatelet, and a beta-blocker for rate control. Each agent has accumulated evidence in younger populations or in trials with limited representation of patients over eighty. Recent randomised trials such as STEP and the ongoing PRESERVE-OLD studies have begun to address the evidence gap, with implications for blood pressure targets in older patients that may favour somewhat higher targets than in younger adults to reduce orthostatic risk while preserving cardiovascular benefit.

Antithrombotic therapy in the elderly carries a steeply rising bleeding risk, as falls, frailty, polypharmacy, declining renal function, and a higher prevalence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy all amplify the haemorrhagic hazard. The decision to anticoagulate an elderly patient with atrial fibrillation is a careful weighing of stroke prevention against an elevated bleeding cost.

Strontium ranelate, formerly used for osteoporosis, was found to increase the risk of myocardial infarction and serious cutaneous reactions including DRESS syndrome, leading to severe restriction of its use and its eventual withdrawal from many markets. Its trajectory illustrates how post-marketing surveillance can uncover hazards that reverse the benefit-risk balance of a drug years after approval.

Praziquantel, the standard treatment for schistosomiasis and many other helminth infections, produces dose-related abdominal pain, dizziness, and headache that are partly attributable to the drug and partly to the inflammatory response from dying parasites. In cysticercosis, the inflammatory response in the central nervous system to dying cysts may produce seizures and increased intracranial pressure, often requiring corticosteroid cover. Therapeutic outcomes can be excellent but management of post-treatment inflammation in neurocysticercosis requires careful titration of immunosuppressive support.

Macrolides including erythromycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin prolong the QT interval and have been associated with sudden cardiac death, particularly in patients with underlying conduction abnormalities or concurrent QT-prolonging agents. Cholestatic hepatitis is an uncommon but well-documented reaction. Drug interactions through CYP3A4 inhibition are clinically important with clarithromycin and erythromycin and considerably less so with azithromycin.

Prescribing cascade is a recognised hazard in geriatric medicine where an adverse drug reaction is misinterpreted as a new condition and treated with an additional drug. Calcium channel blockers cause peripheral oedema mistaken for heart failure and treated with diuretics; metoclopramide produces parkinsonian features treated with levodopa; cholinesterase inhibitors produce urinary incontinence treated with antimuscarinics. Recognition of cascades requires a systematic review of medications introduced in temporal proximity to symptoms, and pharmacist-led medication reviews have demonstrated benefit in identifying and reversing such cascades.

Artemisinin combination therapies are the foundation of contemporary malaria treatment and are generally remarkably safe. Mild gastrointestinal upset, headache, and dizziness are the predominant adverse effects. The Q-T interval is mildly prolonged with several combinations and accumulates with concurrent antiemetics or fluoroquinolones. Delayed-onset haemolytic anaemia occurring weeks after intravenous artesunate has been recognised in severe malaria management, with a recommended monitoring schedule of haemoglobin for at least four weeks after treatment. The recent emergence of artemisinin partial resistance in Southeast Asia and East Africa is the more pressing population-level concern.

Thalidomide is the most consequential teratogen in modern pharmacologic history. Marketed in the late nineteen fifties for nausea in pregnancy, it produced limb reduction defects, particularly phocomelia, cardiac malformations, and a range of other organ system anomalies in approximately ten thousand exposed pregnancies before its withdrawal. The catastrophe transformed regulatory drug approval and was the immediate impetus for the requirement of adequate evidence of safety in pregnancy. Thalidomide has since been rehabilitated for use in multiple myeloma and complications of leprosy, with rigid pregnancy prevention programmes.

Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist used in rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis, produces transaminitis and dyslipidaemia warranting baseline and periodic laboratory monitoring. Suppression of acute-phase response masks the febrile and inflammatory signature of serious infections, with bacterial sepsis, gastrointestinal perforation in patients with diverticular disease, and reactivation of latent infections recognised concerns. Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia are dose-dependent and reversible. Cytokine release syndrome in chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy has become a primary indication, where tocilizumab is itself used as a therapeutic agent.

Postoperative cognitive dysfunction, a measurable decline in memory and executive function persisting days to weeks after major surgery, is most pronounced in elderly patients and those with pre-existing cognitive impairment. Whether the anaesthetic agents themselves, the surgical inflammatory response, or the underlying patient vulnerability is the dominant cause remains debated, and the condition has substantial implications for the perioperative management of an ageing surgical population.

Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic, producing cardiac, craniofacial, and central nervous system malformations in exposed pregnancies. Regulatory pregnancy prevention programmes in the European Union and the United States require pregnancy testing before each prescription, concurrent use of two effective methods of contraception, and prescriber registration. Despite these safeguards, exposed pregnancies still occur and demonstrate the limits of pharmacovigilance dependent on patient cooperation rather than on biological barriers to exposure.

Hyperglycaemia is common during parenteral nutrition because of the concentrated dextrose infusion, and it is associated with increased infectious complications and mortality if uncontrolled. Conversely, abrupt cessation of the infusion can produce rebound hypoglycaemia, since endogenous insulin secretion remains elevated, so parenteral nutrition is generally tapered rather than stopped suddenly.

Griseofulvin, an older oral antifungal for dermatophyte infections that has been largely displaced by terbinafine, induces CYP3A4 and reduces the efficacy of oral contraceptives, an interaction less prominent with the newer agents. Headache, gastrointestinal upset, and photosensitivity are common. Disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol have been reported. Prolonged courses for stubborn nail infections produced cumulative adverse effects that contributed to its decline in practice, although it retains a niche in some paediatric dermatophyte indications where dosing experience is favourable.

Itraconazole, although effective in dermatophytes and selected systemic mycoses, has a complex pharmacokinetic profile with erratic oral absorption that depends on gastric acidity. Negative inotropy through calcium-channel effects on cardiac myocytes contraindicates its use in patients with ventricular dysfunction. Hepatotoxicity may be severe enough to require liver transplantation in rare cases, and the drug carries one of the most extensive lists of pharmacokinetic interactions through CYP3A4 inhibition of any commonly prescribed antifungal. Adrenal suppression mimicking primary insufficiency has been described in long courses.

The combination of methadone or buprenorphine with benzodiazepines or alcohol substantially raises the risk of fatal respiratory depression, and a large fraction of deaths in maintenance populations involve such polysubstance use rather than the opioid alone. This interaction complicates the management of patients with co-occurring anxiety disorders, in whom the prescription of a benzodiazepine carries a meaningful mortality cost.

Contamination or mislabelling of medications compounded or drawn up in advance has caused clusters of perioperative harm, and the storage of concentrated electrolyte solutions, particularly potassium chloride, in clinical areas has led to fatal accidental administration. Removing concentrated potassium from ward and theatre stock is a well-established system response to this specific error.

Allopurinol, used to lower serum urate and prevent gout, can paradoxically precipitate an acute gout flare when started, because the falling urate level mobilises crystals from tissue deposits. Urate-lowering therapy is therefore conventionally accompanied by prophylactic anti-inflammatory cover during the initial months to forestall this counterintuitive flare.

Pharmacokinetic interactions through CYP3A4 inhibition produce some of the most clinically important drug-drug interactions. Strong inhibitors including ritonavir, ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, and grapefruit juice can elevate exposure of substrates such as midazolam, simvastatin, calcineurin inhibitors, and direct-acting oral anticoagulants by manyfold, with attendant toxicity. The clinical task is identification of substrates with narrow therapeutic indices and either avoidance, dose reduction, or therapeutic drug monitoring. Substrate-by-substrate management is now codified in many electronic prescribing systems but human review remains necessary for less common combinations.

Fluconazole at doses used for vaginal candidiasis is generally very well tolerated, but the higher doses required for cryptococcal disease, oesophageal candidiasis, and prophylaxis in immunocompromised populations may produce hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, and the cumulative risk of CYP3A4 inhibition with co-administered substrates. A first-trimester pregnancy exposure carries a small but well-characterised teratogenic risk including craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities at high doses; single low doses for vaginal candidiasis are widely considered safer though not unequivocally so on contemporary data.

Manganese accumulation can occur during prolonged parenteral nutrition, since the metal is supplied in trace-element mixtures but is normally excreted in bile, a route impaired in cholestatic patients. Deposition in the basal ganglia produces a parkinsonian movement disorder visible as increased signal on magnetic resonance imaging, and trace-element provision must be adjusted to prevent this neurotoxic build-up.

Treatment of myxoedema coma with thyroid hormone requires careful judgement, since aggressive replacement in a profoundly hypothyroid patient with depressed adrenal reserve can precipitate an adrenal crisis, and rapid correction can strain a compromised myocardium. Glucocorticoid cover is given alongside hormone replacement specifically to forestall the adrenal complication.

Compounding errors in parenteral nutrition formulations have caused serious harm, including precipitation of calcium and phosphate into insoluble crystals that can embolise to the lung, and contamination events that produced clusters of bloodstream infection. The complexity of these admixtures makes them a recognised high-risk preparation requiring stringent pharmacy controls.

Mefloquine, used in both prophylaxis and treatment of malaria, carries a substantial neuropsychiatric adverse effect burden including vivid dreams, anxiety, depression, paranoia, and rarely psychosis that may persist for weeks or months after discontinuation. A history of psychiatric disease, seizure disorder, or cardiac conduction abnormality contraindicates use. Several military medicine authorities have substantially restricted the agent because of the cumulative experience of psychiatric morbidity in deployed personnel, and alternatives such as atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline have become preferred in most travel medicine practice.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Adeno-associated virus gene therapy targeting the retina, although delivered locally and at low dose, can produce intraocular inflammation, and the surgical subretinal delivery itself carries risks of retinal damage. Even a localised gene therapy thus combines an immunological adverse effect of the vector with a procedural complication of its administration.

Carbimazole and propylthiouracil used in hyperthyroidism share a small but important risk of agranulocytosis, typically occurring within the first three months of treatment. Patients must be counselled to seek immediate medical evaluation for fever, sore throat, or oral ulceration during this period. Propylthiouracil is additionally associated with severe hepatotoxicity, particularly in children, leading to its restriction to second-line use in non-pregnant patients. ANCA-associated vasculitis is a rare but recognised adverse outcome of prolonged thionamide therapy.

Bacterial contamination of blood components, more common with platelets because they are stored at room temperature, can produce a fulminant septic transfusion reaction with high fever, rigors, and shock. The contamination may originate from donor skin flora or asymptomatic donor bacteraemia, and septic platelet transfusion remains a recognised cause of transfusion-related death.

Spontaneous adverse event reporting systems including the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System and the European EudraVigilance database generate signals that may indicate previously unrecognised drug toxicities. Reporting is voluntary and substantially under-represents actual event rates, but disproportionality analyses can identify signals deserving formal evaluation. The detection of fluoroquinolone-associated aortic aneurysm and dissection, of the cardiovascular signal for rofecoxib, and of the heart valve disease associated with fenfluramine all arose from pharmacovigilance review of these databases, sometimes years after marketing.

Belatacept, a costimulation blocker offering an alternative to calcineurin inhibitors and avoiding their nephrotoxicity, carries an important restriction: it markedly increases the risk of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, particularly central nervous system disease, in recipients who are Epstein-Barr virus seronegative at the time of transplant. The drug is therefore contraindicated in that population, illustrating how a viral serostatus dictates the safety of an immunosuppressant.

Antihistamines with anticholinergic activity contribute to the cumulative anticholinergic burden in older adults, and epidemiological studies have linked sustained exposure to this burden with an increased long-term risk of cognitive decline and dementia. The widespread over-the-counter availability of sedating antihistamines as sleep aids means this exposure often occurs without medical oversight.

Residual neuromuscular blockade after general anaesthesia, defined by a train-of-four ratio below the accepted threshold, impairs airway protection and the ventilatory response to hypoxia, predisposing the patient to aspiration and respiratory failure in the recovery room. Studies using objective quantitative monitoring have shown this complication to be far more frequent than clinician estimation suggests, even when reversal agents have been administered.

subtopic: wound care and topical antiseptic toxicity
sentence: Chlorhexidine, a widely used skin antiseptic, is an increasingly recognised cause of anaphylaxis, particularly when it contacts mucosal surfaces or is applied to broken skin, as occurs with chlorhexidine-impregnated central venous catheters. Because the exposure is often regarded as trivial, the antiseptic is frequently overlooked as the culprit in perioperative anaphylaxis.

Drug-induced syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, caused by agents including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and carbamazepine, produces a euvolaemic hyponatraemia through impaired free water excretion. In the elderly the slow development of the low sodium may be missed until it presents with a fall, confusion, or a seizure.

Levonorgestrel emergency contraception is highly safe with predominantly nausea, vomiting, and irregular menstrual bleeding as adverse effects. The agent is less effective in women with higher body mass index, prompting consideration of ulipristal acetate or copper intrauterine device insertion as more reliable alternatives. Concurrent use of enzyme-inducing medications including some antiepileptics and rifampicin reduces efficacy and may necessitate a higher dose or alternative method. The drug is not abortifacient and has no effect on an established pregnancy.

Drug-induced prolongation of the QT interval reflects blockade of the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current, encoded by the hERG channel, and it predisposes to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into fibrillation. Many structurally unrelated drugs share an affinity for this channel, which is why the QT hazard cuts across antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, antibiotics, and antiemetics alike.

Inhaled anticholinergics such as tiotropium and ipratropium produce dry mouth and, when the aerosol contacts the eye, can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in anatomically predisposed patients, particularly when delivered by nebuliser with a loose-fitting mask. Urinary retention may emerge in older men with prostatic enlargement, and the early observational signal of increased cardiovascular events with one delivery device prompted considerable scrutiny before being attributed to the device rather than the drug.

Selective COX-2 inhibitors were developed to retain anti-inflammatory effect while sparing gastrointestinal mucosa, but the cardiovascular safety of this class was called into question by the withdrawal of rofecoxib in two thousand four following the demonstration of increased myocardial infarction risk. Subsequent analyses have suggested that all NSAIDs except possibly naproxen carry some degree of cardiovascular risk, prompting current guidance to use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary period in patients with established or elevated cardiovascular risk.

Serotonin syndrome arises from the simultaneous use of multiple serotonergic agents and presents with neuromuscular hyperactivity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status. Combinations of monoamine oxidase inhibitors with SSRIs are the prototypical and most severe form, but combinations of two SSRIs, SSRIs with tramadol, with linezolid, with methylene blue, or with St John's wort have all produced fatal cases. The neuroleptic malignant syndrome shares features but is precipitated by dopamine antagonists rather than serotonergic agents, and the two require careful distinction at presentation given different management.

Opioid metabolites can accumulate dangerously in renal failure. Morphine is metabolised to morphine-6-glucuronide, an active and renally cleared metabolite whose accumulation produces prolonged sedation and respiratory depression, while normeperidine, a metabolite of meperidine, accumulates to provoke seizures. These metabolite hazards make alternative opioids preferable in significant renal impairment.

The antidepressant discontinuation syndrome, most pronounced with short-half-life serotonergic agents such as paroxetine and venlafaxine, produces dizziness, electric-shock sensations, nausea, irritability, and vivid dreams within days of stopping. The symptoms can be distressing and are sometimes misinterpreted as relapse of the underlying depression, leading patients and clinicians to conclude wrongly that the drug remains necessary.

Live attenuated vaccines including MMR, varicella, and oral typhoid are contraindicated in patients receiving substantial immunosuppression because of the risk of disseminated infection from the vaccine strain. Severely immunocompromised household contacts of patients are generally not at risk from the typical childhood live vaccines, but special precautions apply to the oral polio vaccine and certain adenovirus and smallpox products that shed viable virus.

Bisphosphonates used in osteoporosis are generally well tolerated when administered with adequate hydration and an upright posture, but oesophagitis, oesophageal stricture, and rarely oesophageal carcinoma have been reported. Osteonecrosis of the jaw is a rare complication of long-term use, with the highest risk in patients receiving high intravenous doses for malignancy-related bone disease and after invasive dental procedures. Atypical femoral fractures with a transverse subtrochanteric pattern may complicate prolonged oral bisphosphonate use after about five years.

Abatacept, a CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein that blocks T-cell co-stimulation, has a relatively favourable infection profile compared with TNF inhibitors, with notably lower rates of tuberculosis reactivation, although screening remains recommended. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease patients have been reported to experience exacerbations on treatment, prompting cautious use in that population. Malignancy risk has not been clearly elevated in registry data spanning over a decade, but limitations in long-term observational power are recognised. Pre-existing solid organ transplant is generally a contraindication.

Risk evaluation and mitigation strategies, abbreviated REMS in the United States and broadly paralleled by additional risk minimisation measures in European jurisdictions, attempt to reduce serious risk through restricted distribution, mandatory prescriber training, or patient enrolment in monitoring programmes. Clozapine, isotretinoin, thalidomide, and certain opioid extended-release formulations are subject to such programmes. The effectiveness of REMS is mixed, with adherence to laboratory monitoring schedules variable and inadvertent exposure to teratogenic agents continuing despite the structural barriers intended to prevent it.

Polyethylene glycol bowel preparations used before colonoscopy are generally well tolerated but may produce transient hyponatraemia particularly in elderly patients with diminished renal water excretion. Sodium phosphate-based preparations have largely been displaced from routine use after recognition of acute phosphate nephropathy, a cause of chronic kidney injury that may not present for weeks and that is more frequent in elderly women, those with reduced renal function, and patients on medications that interfere with sodium-phosphate handling. Cardiac arrhythmias from severe potassium and magnesium disturbance have also been reported.

Cholestyramine and other bile acid sequestrants used in cholestatic pruritus and dyslipidaemia are not systemically absorbed and have a benign safety profile in themselves, but they bind a wide range of co-administered medications including warfarin, levothyroxine, digoxin, and fat-soluble vitamins. Constipation, bloating, and steatorrhoea are common dose-limiting effects. The need for staggered dosing of other medications by at least one hour before or four to six hours after the sequestrant complicates regimens substantially.

Perampanel, a non-competitive AMPA receptor antagonist, has shown efficacy in focal and primary generalised tonic-clonic seizures but carries a black box warning for serious psychiatric and behavioural adverse effects including homicidal ideation, hostility, and aggression. These effects are dose-related and most prominent at doses above eight milligrams daily. Slow titration and avoidance in patients with significant psychiatric comorbidity are recommended. Somnolence and dizziness are dose-limiting at lower doses. The agent is also associated with weight gain and rare reports of hepatotoxicity.

Pyrrolizidine alkaloids present in comfrey and certain herbal teas produce a dose-dependent hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, formerly termed veno-occlusive disease, that can progress to portal hypertension and liver failure. Outbreaks have followed contamination of food crops with alkaloid-bearing weeds, and the latency between exposure and clinical presentation often prevents patients and clinicians from identifying the causative agent.

Drugs that interfere with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, predispose to hyperkalaemia, and the risk multiplies when these agents are combined or used in patients with renal impairment. The resulting hyperkalaemia can produce dangerous cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrest.

Mirabegron, a beta-3 adrenergic agonist for overactive bladder developed partly to avoid the anticholinergic effects of older agents, instead produces dose-related increases in blood pressure and heart rate and is cautioned against in patients with poorly controlled hypertension. Urinary retention has been reported when it is combined with antimuscarinic agents, and the drug inhibits the metabolism of certain co-administered substrates.

Metformin's dose-limiting effects in routine practice are gastrointestinal, with nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhoea reported in up to a third of patients on initiation. The slow titration of extended-release formulations substantially mitigates these effects. Lactic acidosis remains a rare but potentially fatal complication, most often in the setting of acute kidney injury, dehydration, or concurrent severe illness; the drug is held during contrast administration in patients with reduced eGFR.

Acute dystonic reactions to dopamine antagonists appear within hours to days of exposure and produce sustained, often painful muscle contractions, including oculogyric crisis, torticollis, and laryngeal spasm that can compromise the airway. The reactions respond rapidly to anticholinergic medication, and their dramatic and frightening presentation in young patients is a classic emergency-department recognition challenge.

Benzodiazepines produce dose-dependent sedation, anterograde amnesia, and impairment of psychomotor performance that may persist into the following day with long-half-life agents such as diazepam. Chronic use leads to tolerance, physiological dependence, and a withdrawal syndrome on abrupt discontinuation that can include seizures, particularly when taken in high doses or for prolonged periods. Tapering over weeks to months is generally required.

Certain drugs produce a hepatotoxicity that closely resembles autoimmune hepatitis, with positive autoantibodies and a histology of interface hepatitis, and these drug-induced autoimmune-like injuries may require corticosteroid treatment in addition to drug withdrawal. Nitrofurantoin and minocycline taken over long periods are recognised causes of this particular pattern.

Diffusion hypoxia can occur at the end of a nitrous oxide anaesthetic, as the large volume of nitrous oxide rapidly leaving the blood and entering the alveoli dilutes alveolar oxygen. Administering supplemental oxygen during emergence is the standard precaution against this transient but real hypoxic hazard.

Metabolic bone disease develops in many patients on long-term parenteral nutrition, with osteoporosis and osteomalacia driven by a combination of aluminium contamination of components, abnormalities of calcium and vitamin D metabolism, and the underlying disease. Bone pain and fragility fractures can result, and the contribution of trace contaminants illustrates how the manufacturing of the nutrition itself can carry skeletal toxicity.

P-glycoprotein-mediated efflux interactions, increasingly recognised alongside cytochrome P450 interactions, affect substrates including digoxin, dabigatran, and certain direct-acting antivirals. Verapamil and amiodarone are clinically important P-glycoprotein inhibitors that can elevate digoxin concentrations sufficient to provoke arrhythmia and gastrointestinal toxicity. The interactive contribution of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein for many substrates means that interaction lists derived from a single mechanism may underestimate clinical risk, and consultation of comprehensive interaction databases is essential for high-risk combinations.

Topical fluoroquinolones used for bacterial conjunctivitis and corneal ulcers may produce corneal crystalline deposits with ciprofloxacin, particularly when used at high frequency for large epithelial defects. These deposits, although alarming clinically, generally resolve after cessation. Tendon adverse effects of systemic fluoroquinolones are not produced by topical use, but allergic conjunctivitis and contact dermatitis of the eyelids may complicate prolonged courses. Antibiotic stewardship is increasingly emphasised given the emergence of resistant Pseudomonas and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Ondansetron and other 5-HT3 receptor antagonists used in chemotherapy-induced and post-operative nausea produce dose-dependent QT prolongation, particularly with the intravenous formulation. Maximum single intravenous doses have been restricted in line with this concern. Constipation, headache, and transaminase elevation are commonly observed. Serotonin syndrome may complicate combination with other serotonergic agents, although the risk with 5-HT3 antagonists is comparatively low. The newer NK1 antagonists such as aprepitant interact through CYP3A4 induction and require dose adjustment of co-administered substrates.

Lacosamide, a newer sodium-channel modulator used in focal epilepsy, produces dose-dependent PR interval prolongation and may precipitate atrial fibrillation in susceptible patients. Baseline electrocardiography is recommended, particularly in patients with known conduction abnormalities or concurrent PR-prolonging medications. Dizziness, diplopia, and ataxia are dose-related and respond to dose reduction. The intravenous formulation is useful in seizure clusters and status epilepticus. Pharmacokinetic interactions are minimal, contributing to its place in polypharmacy regimens where other interactions are problematic.

Acute kidney injury during an intercurrent illness can transform a previously safe medication regimen into a dangerous one overnight, as drugs that were adequately cleared accumulate. The combination of a renin-angiotensin inhibitor, a diuretic, and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, sometimes called the triple whammy, is a recognised precipitant of acute kidney injury that then compounds the problem by impairing the clearance of other agents.

Incomplete reversal of neuromuscular blockade leaves patients with residual weakness that compromises pharyngeal coordination and the protective airway reflexes, a hazard that is invisible to clinical assessment and detectable only by quantitative train-of-four monitoring. The mismatch between apparent recovery and true neuromuscular function is a recurring cause of avoidable respiratory morbidity in the postoperative period.

First-generation antihistamines are a leading cause of accidental and intentional overdose, and in children the toxic ingestion produces an anticholinergic toxidrome with agitation, hallucinations, hyperthermia, and seizures. Diphenhydramine overdose can additionally produce sodium channel blockade with QRS widening and ventricular arrhythmia, making it a more dangerous ingestion than its over-the-counter status suggests.

Sodium phosphate bowel preparations used before colonoscopy have caused severe hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, and an acute phosphate nephropathy, particularly in elderly patients and those with renal impairment or volume depletion. The recognition of this hazard has led to restrictions on the use of these preparations in vulnerable patients.

The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion can be drug-induced, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, carbamazepine, and certain chemotherapeutic agents among the recognised causes. The resulting hyponatraemia may develop insidiously and present with confusion, falls, or seizures, particularly in elderly patients, and is reversed by identifying and withdrawing the responsible medication.

Combined oral contraceptives increase the risk of venous thromboembolism approximately two- to fourfold over baseline, with the magnitude depending on the progestogen component. Drospirenone, desogestrel, and gestodene preparations carry slightly higher absolute risk than levonorgestrel-containing pills. Risk is concentrated in the first year of use, in patients with hereditary thrombophilia, in older smokers, and during the postpartum period. Arterial thrombotic events including myocardial infarction and stroke are concentrated in smokers and patients with migraine with aura. Routine thrombophilia screening is not recommended; family history guides risk-benefit discussions.

Abrupt cessation of clonidine, a centrally acting antihypertensive, produces a rebound hypertensive crisis with headache, agitation, and sometimes encephalopathy, driven by a surge of sympathetic outflow. The reaction is severe enough that clonidine withdrawal is a recognised cause of hypertensive emergency, and the drug must be tapered or substituted carefully, particularly around surgery when oral intake is interrupted.

Calcium and vitamin D supplementation, although widely used for bone health, carries the risk of hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria when doses are excessive, and some analyses have suggested a modest increase in kidney stones and possibly cardiovascular events with high-dose calcium supplements. The therapeutic margin is narrower than the over-the-counter availability of these products implies.

Drug-induced parkinsonism, produced by dopamine-blocking and dopamine-depleting agents, is clinically indistinguishable from idiopathic Parkinson disease in many patients and is frequently misdiagnosed, leading to the inappropriate initiation of antiparkinsonian therapy rather than withdrawal of the causative drug. The symptoms usually improve over weeks to months after the offending agent is stopped.

Statin therapy in older adults remains a contested area. Secondary prevention in patients with established cardiovascular disease is supported by trial data extending into the elderly, with the proviso that absolute benefit is delayed and patients with limited life expectancy may not realise net benefit. Primary prevention in adults over seventy-five lacks definitive randomised evidence, and the recent STAREE trial is expected to inform this gap. Muscle symptoms, although not clearly more frequent in older patients, may have greater functional consequences, and the lowest effective dose with risk-stratified prescribing is the current pragmatic approach.

Intravesical chemotherapy with agents such as mitomycin C following transurethral resection of bladder tumour can produce a chemical cystitis, and inadvertent extravasation through an unrecognised bladder perforation has caused severe pelvic tissue necrosis and fistula formation. Systemic absorption is normally minimal, but a damaged urothelium can permit enough uptake to produce myelosuppression.

Bleeding is the dominant and unavoidable adverse effect of all antithrombotic therapy, since the same inhibition of clot formation that prevents pathological thrombosis also impairs the haemostatic response to vascular injury. Major bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, is the principal harm that must be weighed against the thrombotic benefit for every anticoagulant and antiplatelet drug.

Topical timolol and other non-selective beta-blockers used in primary open-angle glaucoma can produce clinically meaningful systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct, sufficient to provoke bradycardia, bronchospasm, and worsening of heart failure in susceptible patients. Nasolacrimal occlusion for two minutes after instillation substantially reduces systemic exposure. Even in selected patients with asthma, the cardio-selective betaxolol may not be entirely safe and any beta-blocking ophthalmic agent should be used cautiously.

subtopic: gene therapy and viral vector toxicity
sentence: Patients who have received a viral vector gene therapy may mount an immune response that precludes re-treatment with the same vector serotype, so that a suboptimal initial result cannot simply be supplemented with a further dose. This single-shot constraint, imposed by the immune response to the vector, is itself a limitation that behaves like an adverse effect.

The challenge of transplant immunosuppression is that every adjustment trades one harm for another: intensifying the regimen reduces rejection but increases infection and malignancy, while reducing it risks graft loss. This bidirectional hazard means that the optimal regimen is not a fixed prescription but a continuously rebalanced compromise informed by drug levels, biopsy findings, infectious episodes, and the time elapsed since transplantation.

Tardive syndromes extend beyond classic dyskinesia to include tardive dystonia, tardive akathisia, and tardive tremor, all sharing the feature of emerging late in treatment and persisting after drug withdrawal. Tardive dystonia, often affecting the neck and trunk, can be more disabling than the orofacial dyskinesia and is particularly resistant to treatment.

Transfusion-related acute lung injury is a serious complication characterised by the abrupt onset of hypoxaemic respiratory failure within six hours of transfusion, attributed to antibodies in donor plasma or to biologically active lipids that prime the recipient's neutrophils. Preferential use of plasma from male donors has reduced its incidence, since multiparous female donors are more likely to carry the implicated antibodies.

Desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent can react with volatile anaesthetics to generate carbon monoxide, and cases of clinically significant carbon monoxide exposure have occurred in patients anaesthetised with an absorbent that had dried out, typically after a high flow of gas through an unused circuit over a weekend. The hazard is one of equipment and absorbent management rather than the anaesthetic itself.

Denosumab, a monoclonal antibody against RANK ligand used for osteoporosis, produces a profound rebound increase in bone turnover when discontinued, and multiple vertebral fractures have occurred in the months after a missed or stopped dose. This rebound phenomenon means that denosumab cannot simply be stopped and requires transition to an alternative antiresorptive agent, a striking example of a withdrawal effect dictating prescribing.

Topiramate, used in migraine prophylaxis, produces cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty that patients describe vividly, along with paraesthesiae, weight loss, and an increased risk of renal stones through carbonic anhydrase inhibition. It can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma and is teratogenic, producing oral clefts, which constrains its use in women of childbearing potential.

Corticosteroids form part of most transplant immunosuppression regimens and contribute substantially to the long-term morbidity of transplantation through new-onset diabetes, osteoporosis with avascular necrosis of the femoral head, cataract, hypertension, and cushingoid body habitus. Steroid-sparing and steroid-withdrawal protocols have been developed specifically to limit this cumulative toxicity while maintaining adequate rejection prophylaxis.

Calcitonin gene-related peptide antagonists developed for migraine, including the monoclonal antibodies and the small-molecule gepants, have a generally favourable tolerability profile, but constipation can be marked with one of the antibodies, and post-marketing reports of hypertension have prompted scrutiny. Because the CGRP pathway has roles in cardiovascular and gastrointestinal physiology, long-term safety surveillance of these agents remains ongoing.

Metformin accumulation in the setting of acute kidney injury is the principal mechanism behind metformin-associated lactic acidosis, a rare but serious complication. Because the kidney is the sole route of metformin elimination, any abrupt decline in renal function, as may follow dehydration or sepsis, can allow the drug to rise to concentrations that impair mitochondrial respiration.

Paracetamol hepatotoxicity is the archetype of intrinsic, dose-dependent drug-induced liver injury, in which a reactive metabolite overwhelms hepatic glutathione and produces centrilobular necrosis predictable from the dose ingested. It contrasts sharply with idiosyncratic injury, which is unpredictable, not clearly dose-related, and dependent on host factors that are only partially understood.

Abrupt discontinuation of long-term beta-blocker therapy can precipitate a rebound syndrome of tachycardia, hypertension, and worsening angina, attributed to upregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors during chronic blockade. Myocardial infarction has followed sudden cessation in patients with coronary disease, and gradual tapering over one to two weeks is therefore recommended rather than stopping the drug outright.

Romosozumab, a sclerostin inhibitor used for severe osteoporosis, was found in one large trial to be associated with an excess of cardiovascular events including myocardial infarction and stroke compared with an active comparator. This unexpected cardiovascular signal led to a boxed warning and a contraindication in patients with recent cardiovascular events, constraining the use of an otherwise potent bone-forming agent.

Domperidone, a peripherally acting dopamine antagonist used as an antiemetic and prokinetic, prolongs the QT interval and has been associated with sudden cardiac death, particularly at higher doses and in older patients. Regulatory authorities have responded by restricting the dose and duration of treatment and contraindicating it in patients with cardiac conduction disturbances or significant electrolyte abnormalities.

JAK inhibitors including tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib carry a class-wide regulatory warning following the ORAL Surveillance trial that demonstrated higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events, malignancy, venous thromboembolism, and all-cause mortality compared with TNF inhibitors in patients with rheumatoid arthritis over fifty with a cardiovascular risk factor. Lymphopenia, anaemia, herpes zoster reactivation at substantially elevated rates, and laboratory abnormalities including elevated creatine kinase and lipids are commonly observed. Pre-treatment zoster vaccination is now recommended where possible.

Desmopressin used for nocturnal polyuria and nocturnal enuresis acts as a vasopressin analogue and carries a clear risk of dilutional hyponatraemia, which can produce confusion, seizures, and death, particularly in older patients and when fluid intake is not restricted around dosing. The narrowing of its licensed indications and the requirement for serum sodium monitoring in older users reflect the seriousness of this electrolyte hazard.

The recognition of nitrosamine contaminants in valsartan and several other angiotensin receptor blockers in two thousand eighteen led to multinational recalls and increased regulatory scrutiny of manufacturing processes. Nitrosamine impurities including NDMA and NDEA are probable human carcinogens at sufficient exposures. Investigation has subsequently identified similar contaminants in ranitidine, metformin, and varenicline, with corresponding regulatory actions. The episode highlights the importance of process chemistry and the limits of conventional impurity testing protocols in identifying novel contaminants at trace concentrations.

Insulin and beta-agonists drive potassium into cells and can produce acute hypokalaemia, a property exploited therapeutically in the treatment of hyperkalaemia but capable of causing dangerous potassium depletion when high-dose beta-agonist therapy is used for asthma or when insulin is given to a patient who is not truly hyperkalaemic.

Concentrated grapefruit juice irreversibly inhibits intestinal cytochrome P450 3A4 by suppressing enzyme expression, an effect that persists for a day or more after a single exposure. The resulting increase in oral bioavailability has produced clinically dangerous elevations in plasma concentrations of simvastatin, certain calcium channel blockers, and some immunosuppressants, with reported rhabdomyolysis and profound hypotension attributable to this dietary interaction.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a paradoxical and dangerous adverse effect in which antibodies against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets, producing thrombocytopenia together with arterial and venous thrombosis rather than bleeding. Recognition demands immediate cessation of all heparin and substitution of a non-heparin anticoagulant.

Hydroquinone, used in cosmetic depigmenting preparations for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, may produce paradoxical exogenous ochronosis with prolonged or high-concentration use, characterised by a blue-black confluent discoloration that may be irreversible. The condition is particularly described in darker skin types in regions where unregulated high-concentration preparations are available. Several European regulatory authorities have therefore restricted hydroquinone in over-the-counter cosmetic products and limit its use to prescription dermatologic indications under medical supervision.

Local granuloma formation at the site of adjuvanted vaccine injection, particularly with repeated dosing in allergen immunotherapy preparations that use aluminium, can produce persistent itchy nodules that last months to years. Some recipients develop a contact allergy to aluminium itself, which then complicates the use of any aluminium-adjuvanted product.

Combinations of nephrotoxic drugs produce additive renal injury that may exceed what either agent would produce alone. The combination of aminoglycosides with vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin, or contrast media all increase nephrotoxic risk substantially. ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and direct renin inhibitors should not be used in combination because of additive renal and hyperkalaemia risk without offsetting benefit. The triple combination of an ACE inhibitor or ARB, an NSAID, and a diuretic in a volume-depleted patient is a recognised and avoidable cause of community-acquired acute kidney injury.

Microvesicular steatosis is a distinctive and dangerous pattern of drug-induced liver injury in which small fat droplets accumulate within hepatocytes as a result of impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation. It is the lesion seen in valproate hepatotoxicity and in the historic syndrome produced by certain antiretroviral nucleoside analogues, and it can be accompanied by lactic acidosis and rapid hepatic failure.

Iodinated contrast media produce two distinct categories of adverse reaction. Immediate hypersensitivity reactions, ranging from urticaria to anaphylaxis, occur within an hour and are not predicted by iodine or shellfish allergy despite the persistence of that clinical myth. Non-immediate reactions, typically delayed maculopapular eruptions appearing one to several days after exposure, reflect a T-cell-mediated mechanism and recur on re-exposure to structurally related agents.
